# Signed polyhedral facet variations are already in the tested physical-cone closure

This checks a proposed enrichment of the NEW H first-variation program. At a fixed polyhedral body, arbitrary sufficiently small offsets of its nonvertical ambient facets are actual admissible variations. Their first-order boundary speeds, including sampled-facet ties, are limits of the globally convex physical fields already tested by the SAME separator. The same statement holds for small rotations of those facets. Thus adding these motions does not by itself supply new linear stress inequalities.

The final section states the separate exact inside-hinge issue, which this closure argument does not settle.

## 1. Actual admissible polyhedral paths

Work in the relative full ambient space of the fixed base affine hull. Let the canonical polyhedral body be

    C={w=(z,x): A_i·w<=b_i, i=1,...,m},
    A_i=(a_i,u_i).

Assume its complete finite sampled base P consists of positive-volume fibers and its projection is conv(P), as in the compact H model. Keep every purely base facet, u_i=0, fixed. For u_i!=0 choose arbitrary coefficients dot A_i,dot b_i and set

    C(t)={w:(A_i+t dot A_i)·w<=b_i+t dot b_i},

with the unaltered constraints for u_i=0. For all sufficiently small signed t, C(t) is bounded and retains a positive own inball in every sampled fiber: the old own inball centers have strict slack against every nonvertical constraint, and there are only finitely many. Boundedness persists because the old full facet-normal system has a positive spanning margin: the minimum over unit v of max_i A_i·v is positive, and stays positive under sufficiently small normal perturbations. This bounds every point of C(t) uniformly using the perturbed inequalities. The constraint errors on that common bounded set are O(|t|). Fix an interior point o with positive slack at every ambient facet. Comparing those errors with the finitely many positive slacks sandwiches C(t) between homothetic copies o+(1±K|t|)(C-o), for a fixed sufficiently large K. Thus the polyhedra remain O(|t|)-close to C.

No new integer base appears for small t: within a fixed bounded neighborhood, the finitely many integer points outside conv(P) have positive distance from it. The fixed pure-base constraints also cannot remove a boundary sampled base. Consequently the sampled families K_z(t)=C(t)_z are actual positive compatible families on the same P. Taking their canonical hull preserves these sampled fibers. No assertion that the combinatorial normal fan remains simple or unchanged is needed.

## 2. Exact sampled-facet speeds, including ties

For every nonvertical facet put

    n_i=u_i/|u_i|,
    g_i(w)=(b_i-A_i·w)/|u_i|>=0 on C,
    v_i(w)=(dot A_i·w-dot b_i)/|u_i|.

Here v_i is the inward speed of that one moving affine constraint. Group indices by the finitely many distinct continuous normals n_i.

At almost every boundary point x of a sampled fiber K_z, the own normal n is unique. Every nonvertical constraint active along the relative interior of that own facet has continuous normal n. If I(z,x) is that active set, the actual inward normal speed of C(t)_z is

    v(z,x)=max_(i in I(z,x)) v_i(z,x)                (right derivative at t=0).

Indeed motion by -t v n gives first-order feasibility v>=v_i for every active constraint, while all inactive constraints retain slack. A common interior radial ray gives the same formula with its positive normal denominator, and yields the ordinary signed shell derivative. Lower-dimensional own edges are surface-null. Pure-base constraints are fixed and impose no continuous boundary speed.

For offsets alone v_i is constant. For rotations it is affine in the full physical point w. In particular ties cannot be treated as linear: replacing a direction by its negative changes max(active v_i) to -min(active v_i), not generally to -v.

## 3. Explicit globally convex approximating fields

Choose B>0 larger than every |v_i(w)| on C. For each distinct normal n_g choose a nonnegative continuous function psi_g on the continuous unit sphere, equal to one at n_g and zero at all other distinct normals; their supports can be disjoint. For T>0 define

    Phi_T(n,w)=sum_g psi_g(n)
          max( -B, max_(i:n_i=n_g)[v_i(w)-T g_i(w)] ).

Every g_i and v_i is affine. Hence Phi_T is continuous, globally finite, and convex in the full physical variable w for each n. It belongs to the already proved physical cone; signed values are allowed there.

On C every maximum is between -B and B. At a sampled boundary point with normal n_g, at least one constraint in that group is active. As T tends to infinity, inactive terms tend to minus infinity and the active terms remain v_i. Therefore

    Phi_T(n_z(x),z,x) -> max_(i in I(z,x))v_i(z,x)

at surface-almost every point. This is a bounded convergence statement on the ACTUAL old normal bundle, not a change of the selected cap or source law.

## 4. Consequence for the SAME H separator

The actual H separator satisfies integral Xi Phi_T dS<=0 for every T. Its response density is integrable (indeed uniformly bounded in the compact proper-source class). Dominated convergence gives

    integral Xi v dS<=0

for the exact polyhedral path velocity from Section 2. All energy, volume and covariance first responses are linear continuous functionals of this bounded speed, so the same passage retains their actual coefficients. Arbitrary signed cap-normal and scale variables were already included and can be retained simultaneously.

If each positive-area sampled facet has a unique active ambient constraint, the speed is linear in the facet parameters and v(-dot b)=-v(dot b). Applying the result to both signs gives the familiar exact facet-by-facet stationarity equalities. They were already consequences of the tested-cone closure, not new constraints. If ties occur, the two resulting inequalities are exactly the max/min speed inequalities and no false equality is inferred.

Thus fixed-normal offsets, their signed versions, and small ambient-facet rotations do not create a genuinely stronger first-order LINEAR separator. Polyhedral approximation also cannot make these closure consequences stronger merely by passing to a limit; preserving actual stationarity under such an approximation remains a separate obligation.

## 5. A different issue remains: the exact inside-support hinge

The existing separator was obtained from a conservative response that retains full inside body capture and omits a favorable inside hinge. Adding more physical velocities does not recover information lost at that earlier step.

At an inside supporting facet, if v is the body inward speed and c=(r-nu·w)/|u| is the cap-plane speed measured toward the captured side, the exact loss is max(v,c). The conservative response retains v. At an outside supporting facet the body inward normal points in the opposite direction, and the exact loss is -[-c-v]_+; this is the actual outside hinge already retained in the proved program. The essential inside distinction is simply max(v,c)=v+[c-v]_+.

For offsets with fixed normals and fixed cap-normal velocities, these are finite piecewise-linear expressions after the threshold/contact variables are included. A chamber-by-chamber analysis of the EXACT response might impose conditions not visible in one conservative linear separator. This note does not prove that it does. Merely taking a Clarke convex hull can instead allow additional inside selectors (body selector 1-tau, section selector tau) and need not strengthen the old conclusion. Any new use must preserve the same actual branch feasibility and quantile equalization across all cap groups.
